items.prompt: In the circuits framework, what is a circuit?
choices: Features connected by weights, forming a computational subgraph
A set of training examples that activate one neuron
A path in the loss landscape between two minima
A sequence of layers with residual connections
items.explain: Zoom In defines circuits as features connected by weights; features are the nodes and weights the edges, read directly from the trained network.

items.prompt: Why do polysemantic neurons undermine reading circuits neuron by neuron?
choices: They only appear in untrained networks
One neuron responds to several unrelated features, so it is not a single feature
items.explain: If one neuron mixes unrelated features, a neuron-level circuit diagram mislabels its nodes; this motivates superposition and dictionary methods.

items.prompt: In toy models of superposition, which change makes a model more likely to store features in superposition?
choices: Adding more hidden dimensions than features
items.explain: Sparse features rarely co-occur, so interference between nearly orthogonal directions is cheap; the toy models show superposition growing with sparsity.

items.prompt: Which established field studies recovering more sparse signals than measured dimensions, and what does it require that learned networks are not known to satisfy?
choices: Compressed sensing; conditions on the measurement operator such as restricted isometry
items.explain: Superposition is related to compressed sensing, whose recovery guarantees need conditions on the sensing operator; a trained network's weights are not known to meet them.

items.prompt: Given the token pattern [A][B] … [A], what does an induction head promote as the next token?
choices: The most frequent token in the context
items.explain: A previous-token head marks what followed each token; the induction head then attends to the token after the earlier [A] and copies [B].

items.prompt: How strong is the evidence that induction heads drive most in-context learning in large models with MLPs, according to the authors themselves?
choices: Proven by ablation in every model size
Mainly correlational; the interventional evidence is for small attention-only models
items.explain: Olsson et al. grade their evidence by model type: causal for small attention-only models, mostly correlational for large models.

items.prompt: In the IOI circuit, what complicates reading a head's importance from an ablation?
choices: GPT-2 small has no attention heads
Backup name-mover heads take over when the main ones are ablated
The task has no correct answer
items.explain: Wang et al. found backup heads that compensate, so a single ablation can understate a component's role.

items.prompt: Which technique was used to isolate the IOI circuit?
items.explain: Path patching, a variant of activation patching that restricts effects to selected paths, located the 26 heads.

items.prompt: What does activation patching measure?
choices: The change in output when an activation is replaced by its value from another input
The gradient of the loss with respect to the weights
The number of parameters in a layer
The entropy of the attention pattern
items.explain: Patching copies an activation from a source run into a target run and measures the effect on a chosen metric.

items.prompt: Hase et al. compared causal-tracing localization with model editing. What did they find?
choices: Editing works only at the localized layer
Localization did not predict which layer was best to edit
Causal tracing cannot be computed for GPT models
items.explain: Knowing where a fact is localized by causal tracing gave little information about where editing it works best.

items.prompt: Attribution patching approximates the patching effect of activation a on metric m as:
items.explain: It is the first-order Taylor term of m around the corrupted activation, computed for every component from one backward pass.

items.prompt: When is a small attribution-patching score weak evidence that a component is unimportant?
choices: When the metric is affine in the activation
When the model is a linear regression
When attention is saturated or paths cancel, so the linear estimate misses the true effect
items.explain: Kramár et al. identify saturated attention softmaxes and cancellation as sources of false negatives.

items.prompt: In causal scrubbing, which activations are resampled from other inputs?
choices: Those the hypothesis claims do not matter for the behaviour
items.explain: The hypothesis determines which activations can be swapped between inputs without changing the behaviour; performance after resampling scores it.

items.prompt: Two incompatible hypotheses both recover most of the loss under causal scrubbing. What follows?
choices: The test does not identify the mechanism on this dataset
items.explain: A pass is consistency with the dataset and metric, not uniqueness; incompatible hypotheses passing shows the test is non-identifying there.

items.prompt: What does an interchange intervention do?
choices: Swaps two layers of the network
Retrains the model on swapped labels
Sets an internal representation to its value on a different input and checks the high-level model's prediction
Exchanges the encoder and decoder of an SAE
items.explain: It tests whether intervening on an aligned internal variable has the effect the high-level causal model predicts.

items.prompt: Why can a learned subspace pass interchange tests yet misrepresent where a feature lives?
choices: The intervention can work by activating a dormant parallel pathway
items.explain: Makelov et al. show subspace patching can produce the right output through a pathway the model does not normally use.

items.prompt: What does ACDC automate?
choices: Pruning edges of the computational graph whose removal barely changes a task metric
items.explain: ACDC iteratively patches edges and removes those below a threshold of effect on the metric.

items.prompt: Which finding about ACDC concerns cost and accuracy?
choices: Edge attribution patching recovered circuits better on average with two forward passes and one backward pass
It always finds a unique circuit regardless of threshold
It replaces the need for a metric
items.explain: Syed, Rager and Conmy report higher average circuit-recovery AUC for the gradient-based method at much lower cost.

items.prompt: What does a sparse autoencoder trained on activations learn?
choices: A low-rank projection with fewer directions than dimensions
An overcomplete dictionary of directions, few of which are active per input
items.explain: SAEs use more latents than dimensions, with a sparsity penalty so each input activates only a few.

items.prompt: SAEs trained on the same model and data but different seeds share only part of their features. Which conclusion fits best?
choices: Seeds should be averaged to get the true features
An SAE's features are one useful decomposition, not a unique list of the model's true features
items.explain: Paulo and Belrose conclude that SAE features are a pragmatically useful decomposition rather than a universal list.

items.prompt: What happened when the Golden Gate Bridge feature was clamped to a high value?
choices: The model's outputs became about the bridge, even identifying as it
The model's loss went to zero
items.explain: Clamping the feature to ten times its maximum activation induced bridge-related behaviour, evidence that the feature influences outputs.

items.prompt: The authors find a feature related to deception. What do they caution?
choices: The feature proves the model lies
Knowing about lies differs from lying, so the feature's existence does not show the behaviour
Deception features appear only in images
items.explain: The paper warns against reading too much into a safety-relevant feature's existence.

items.prompt: How does a transcoder differ from an SAE?
choices: It reconstructs the same activation it reads
It predicts a sublayer's output from that sublayer's input through a sparse hidden layer
It operates on tokens, not activations
items.explain: A transcoder imitates the MLP sublayer's input–output map, which makes feature-to-feature attributions tractable.

items.prompt: A crosscoder diff between a base and a chat model shows chat-only latents. What control would help check them?
choices: A diff between two seeds of the same base model, which should show few model-specific latents
items.explain: Sparsity artefacts can create spurious model-specific latents, so a null diff gives a baseline rate.

items.prompt: Why are edges in an attribution graph linear for a given prompt?
choices: Attention patterns and normalization are frozen, and transcoders bridge the MLP nonlinearities
Only the last layer is used
items.explain: Freezing the remaining nonlinearities makes direct feature-to-feature interactions linear in the local replacement model.

items.prompt: For roughly what share of the prompts they tried did the authors report satisfying insight from attribution graphs?
items.explain: The biology paper states the graphs gave satisfying insight for about a quarter of prompts tried.

items.prompt: What does the causal inner product in Park, Choe and Veitch accomplish?
choices: It makes the probing direction and the steering direction for a concept coincide
items.explain: Under that inner product, the embedding-space and unembedding-space notions of a concept direction agree.

items.prompt: Which finding is a counterexample to the claim that every feature is one-dimensionally linear?
choices: Circular representations of days of the week and months
items.explain: Engels et al. found irreducibly multi-dimensional, circular features.

items.prompt: What is a probe's selectivity?
choices: Accuracy on the linguistic task minus accuracy on a control task with random labels
The number of parameters in the probe
The rank of the probe's weight matrix
items.explain: Control tasks can only be learned by the probe itself, so the difference isolates what the representation contributes.

items.prompt: A probe decodes a property with 95% accuracy. What additional evidence shows the model uses that property?
choices: An intervention along the probe direction that changes behaviour as predicted
Reporting the accuracy on the training set
items.explain: Decodability is correlational; use needs an intervention.

items.prompt: How does the tuned lens differ from the logit lens?
choices: It decodes only the final layer
It learns an affine translator per layer before the unembedding
items.explain: The logit lens applies the unembedding directly; the tuned lens first applies a trained affine map per layer.

items.prompt: Why should a lens reading be treated as a probing result?
choices: Because lenses only work on vision models
Because it shows what a decoder can read from a layer, not what computation the model performs with it
items.explain: A lens is a decoder trained or applied post hoc; information it reads may be unused downstream.

items.prompt: How is an activation-addition steering vector typically built?
choices: From the difference in activations between two contrasting prompts
From the gradient of the loss
items.explain: Activation addition takes the activation difference for a prompt pair and adds it during the forward pass.

items.prompt: On AxBench, which method steered best?
items.explain: Prompting outperformed all representation-based steering methods, followed by fine-tuning; SAEs were not competitive.

items.prompt: What algorithm did the modular-addition network learn?
choices: A lookup table of all pairs
Discrete Fourier components combined with trigonometric identities
items.explain: Nanda et al. reverse-engineered a Fourier multiplication algorithm from the weights.

items.prompt: Why are the progress measures not a general method for predicting emergence in advance?
choices: They were derived from the reverse-engineered mechanism, which must be known first
items.explain: The measures rely on knowing the algorithm, which was found after training in a small, checkable task.

items.prompt: Why did linear probes for Othello-GPT's board fail with black/white labels but succeed later?
choices: The board is linear relative to the player to move (mine/theirs)
Nonlinear probes were mislabelled as linear
items.explain: Nanda, Lee and Wattenberg found a linear representation in a mine/theirs basis.

items.prompt: What makes Othello-GPT stronger evidence than probe accuracy alone?
choices: Editing the decoded board state changes move predictions as expected
items.explain: The intervention shows the model uses the representation, not only that it is decodable.

items.prompt: In belief-state geometry, what is represented linearly in the residual stream?
choices: The posterior belief over the generating HMM's hidden states
items.explain: Shai et al. find the Bayesian belief state over hidden states, as computed from the mixed-state presentation.

items.prompt: What makes the belief-geometry result checkable in a way typical SAE feature labels are not?
choices: The target geometry is computed from the known generator before the network is examined
items.explain: The prediction is fixed in advance from computational mechanics, so the readout is compared with a known answer.

items.prompt: What did Bolukbasi et al. show about interpreting a BERT neuron from its top-activating examples?
choices: Different datasets give different, each convincing, interpretations
items.explain: The interpretation depended on the dataset used to find the examples.

items.prompt: Which practice best guards against interpretability illusions?
choices: Using more top-activating examples from the same dataset
Held-out dataset checks plus interventions whose effects are predicted beforehand
items.explain: Illusions arise from dataset dependence and unintended pathways; out-of-sample checks and predeclared interventions address both.

items.prompt: On out-of-distribution harmful-intent detection, how did SAE probes compare with dense linear probes in the GDM study?
choices: SAE probes underperformed dense linear probes
items.explain: Dense linear probes performed nearly perfectly, including out of distribution; SAE probes were worse.

items.prompt: SAEBench found what about SAE proxy metrics?
choices: Gains on them did not reliably translate into better practical performance
items.explain: Karvonen et al. report that proxy-metric gains do not reliably carry over to practical tasks.

items.prompt: What hidden objective was the audited model trained to have?
choices: Exploiting known errors in RLHF reward models
items.explain: The model learned about reward-model errors and was trained to exploit some of them.

items.prompt: Why does success in this auditing game not show that audits find unplanted objectives?
choices: One objective was planted, partly via searchable documents, and the answer was known to organizers
items.explain: A planted objective with traces in the training data gives auditors routes that an unplanted objective may not.

items.prompt: What objective does OSDT minimize?
choices: Squared error plus an L2 weight penalty
Information gain at the root only
Misclassification error plus λ times the number of leaves
The number of features used, ignoring accuracy
items.explain: OSDT trades training error against a per-leaf penalty and finds the certified optimum.

items.prompt: With threshold guessing from a reference ensemble, optimality is guaranteed relative to what?
items.explain: Guessing restricts the candidate splits; the tree is optimal over that restricted set.

items.prompt: What is the Rashomon set?
choices: The set of models in a class whose loss is within ε of the best
All models with zero training error
items.explain: It collects almost-equally-accurate models from a function class.

items.prompt: The Rashomon ratio and the local learning coefficient both relate to which quantity?
choices: The volume of a near-optimal (sublevel) set of the loss
items.explain: The Rashomon ratio is a volume ratio at fixed ε; the LLC is the exponent of the near-optimal parameter volume as ε → 0. Their relationship is an atlas hypothesis.

items.prompt: What does Rudin (2019) recommend for high-stakes decisions?
choices: Explaining black-box models with saliency maps
Using inherently interpretable models instead of explaining black boxes
items.explain: The paper argues for interpretable models because post-hoc explanations are not fully faithful.

items.prompt: Which scope limits the paper's claim that simple models often match complex ones?
items.explain: The accuracy argument concerns structured data with meaningful features, not raw perceptual data.
